challenge_a: A is strongest because its claim is about demonstrated policy exploration. Replace "makes reinforcement learning useful to Alaska" with "demonstrates a way Alaska researchers can explore harvest choices" so simulated differences do not become an established practical benefit. Its falsifier appropriately targets the reported differences. Keep "smoother policy" distinct from an independently measured claim of smoother catches.
challenge_b: B overreaches in two places. The verified safe set does not explicitly establish that the constant-recruitment comparison delivers steadier catches, so remove that extra assertion unless separately validated. Its conventional-rule falsifier tests exclusive superiority, which its thesis never claims. Equally good conventional alternatives would not erase the value of discovering or examining a learned alternative. Replace that falsifier with failure to reproduce the reported scenario-dependent tradeoffs.
scenario_accuracy: Both correctly separate higher spawning biomass with large catch swings in the constant-recruitment case from smoother learned policy, higher catches and less spawning biomass in the Ricker case. Preserve the comparison baseline in each. Do not animate one deployed policy adapting to a changed ocean; these are distinct simulated experiments.
second_movement: Earned. The Ricker result overturns the tempting inference that the method always purchases stock protection with catch volatility. It adds evidence, not a generic AI warning. B's ending about catch swings alone loses that second movement by excluding the biomass tradeoff.
strongest_revision: Choose A: This pollock study demonstrates a way to explore harvest choices before real seasons: under two recruitment assumptions, learned policies produce different combinations of catch and breeding-stock outcomes. That earns further comparison against explicit management goals, without establishing a winning real-world rule.
